title: Journey from multilateralism to regional collaboration: Nepal, India explores shared stance - The Rising Nepal
description: Journey from multilateralism to regional collaboration: Nepal, India explores shared stance  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct 23: Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle and Indian External Affairs Minister Dr. S. Jaishankar have engaged in a dialogue on forms and future of international collaboration in changing global situation.

At a session held as part of the 'NDTV World Summit 2026' organized by the Indian television channel NDTV, today, the discussion between two leaders focused on changes in the world order, the future of multilateral cooperation, and the need for regional and sub-regional partnerships.

At the summit’s session titled 'The Geopolitics of Sovereign Choice,' Indian Foreign Minister Dr. Jaishankar was the keynote speaker while Finance Minister Dr. Wagle was a guest speaker.

Finance Minister Wagle recalled that the world after the end of the Cold War prioritized multilateralism in trade and economic sectors, but in recent years its foundation has been weakening.

He raised questions about the potential to institutionalize bilateral, trilateral, and regional cooperation in areas like disaster response, nutrition, energy, and clean energy amid the expansion of trade blocs and the rise of global fragmentation.

Dr. Wagle also questioned whether efforts at international cooperation should be strengthened through formal institutional structures or advanced based on mutual understanding between partner countries.

In response, Indian Foreign Minister Jaishankar said that over the past two decades, countries have been emphatically moving towards practical cooperation rather than formal commitments.

According to him, a lot of time can be spent on mutual talks, administrative processes, financial responsibilities, and rule-making while building formal institutional structures.

Noting that such arrangements are suitable where formal structures are necessary, he viewed that not all cooperation needs to be tied to institutional frameworks.

Presenting the International Solar Alliance as an example of formal cooperation, he said the nature of cooperation can vary depending on the topic, partners, and the level of commitment.

Stating that such provisions are appropriate in areas where a formal framework is required, the Finance Minister expressed the view that formal institutional frameworks are necessary in certain areas, but not all forms of cooperation need to be bound by such structures. Citing the International Solar Alliance as an example of formal cooperation, he said that the nature of collaboration can vary depending on agenda, the partners involved, and the level of commitment.

Referring to BRICS, Jaishankar said the grouping does not have its own secretariat and is not a charter signed by all its members. He highlighted the structural differences between BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, adding not all mechanisms for cooperation need a single, uniform framework.

"If you ask me about the trend, I would say, it is clearly shifting towards more ad-hoc arrangements and partnership between like-minded nations," the Indian Minister said.

Recalling that over the past decade, India has formed around 50 such groupings ranging from trilateral and quadrilateral arrangements to alliances of like-minded countries, he said there is a growing interest among nations in a collaboration model which has less administrative costs and capable of giving tangible results.

Prior to this, Finance Minister Wagle applauded India's support to Nepal in the disaster-response efforts following the devastating floods that struck the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river systems on August 26.

He said Nepal is grateful to India for such prompt support provided within hours of the disaster occurrence. He also remembered India's support to Nepal during the 2015 major earthquake.

The dialogues centered on exploring ways for strengthening international cooperation, making it further effective amidst global tensions, economic fragmentation.

The shifting roles of major powers were expected to be an opportunity for the two leaders to exchange views on multilateralism, regional partnerships, and results-oriented diplomacy.(RSS)

title: What is Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD)? - Manorama Yearbook
description: What is Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD)?  Manorama Yearbook
publisher.title: Manorama Yearbook
full_article:
• The Board of the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) has provisionally set aside $21.6 million from its available commitment authority for Nepal.

• The decision was made during the Board’s first-ever extraordinary meeting on October 22.

• The Board has 26 members from Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), and the 2015 Paris Agreement.

• Triggered by a climate-induced ice-and-rock avalanche on August 26, a massive debris flow and severe downstream flooding devastated Nepal’s Bhote Koshi-Trishuli-Narayani river system, claiming many lives and leaving others still missing.

What is FRLD?

• Climate change disproportionately affects developing nations, leading to excessive losses and damage, undermining development progress, exacerbating poverty, displacing populations, and destabilising livelihoods.

• The Conference of the Parties (COP) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement (CMA) established the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) with a mandate to assist developing nations that are particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change in responding to economic and non-economic loss and damage associated with the adverse effects of climate change, including extreme weather events and slow onset events.

• A landmark agreement reached at COP27 in 2022 in Sharm El-Sheikh, Egypt, led to the decision to establish a fund to consolidate global efforts to address climate-induced loss and damage.

• Subsequently, a transitional committee was formed to help design the Fund’s framework.

• During COP28 in 2023 in Dubai, the United Arab Emirates, the COP and CMA decided to operationalise the Fund as an entity entrusted with the operation of the financial mechanism.

• It addresses the growing needs of vulnerable communities in developing countries facing the irreversible impacts of climate change.

• By financing recovery initiatives from climate-related losses and damage, the Fund empowers communities to rebuild and adapt.

• It strives for country-led locally driven solutions, ensuring interventions are aligned to country needs, priorities and contexts.

• A Board of 26 members was constituted in 2023, and subsequently, the Philippines was selected as the host of the Board in 2024, while the World Bank was selected to host the Secretariat, and as the Fund Trustee.

title: Bodies of Missing Japanese Climbers Found on Gangapurna West - Explorersweb »
description: Bodies of Missing Japanese Climbers Found on Gangapurna West  Explorersweb »
publisher.title: Explorersweb »
full_article:
This morning, rescuers found the bodies of Japanese climbers Hidesuke Taneishi, 40, and Tetsu Hashimoto, 25, on Gangapurna West (7,140m).

“Both bodies were found at around 6,300m on the south side of Gangapurna West,” the rescue team told The Tourism Times .

Hidesuke Taneishi (left) and Tetsu Hashimoto (right) with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure

The climbers were attempting the first ascent of the mountain and lost contact on October 15 at approximately 7,050m on their summit push.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Heli/drone search

A search and rescue team has been looking for the pair since October 19. Unfortunately, no one knew where they were on the mountain, or even if they were on the mountain at all. Therefore, the search started at Manang village, with no success.

The team included helicopter pilot Sobit Gauchan, high-altitude photographer and climber Manish Maharjan, and IFMGA mountain guide Pansang Rinzee Sherpa. The helicopter dropped Maharjan and Rinzee at 5,750m, and from there they used a drone to search the upper slopes. They scouted the northeast and southwest sides of the mountain, and finally found the remains of the Japanese climbers’ higher camp. Today, they found the bodies on the south side.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

As for the cause of the accident, Rinzee told ExplorersWeb that their observations of the terrain pointed to a snow slab collapse.

Background

Several teams have attempted Gangapurna West, located next to the Annapurna massif in Manang district, since it opened to foreign teams in 2014. However, none have summited. The mountain is also known as Asapurna or Lachenal Peak.

Team leader Hidesuke Taneishi was nominated for a Piolet d’Or last year after his first ascent of 6,652m Pholesobi Peak, also in Nepal, via a direct route up its vertiginous north face with Hiroki Yamamoto.

title: Himalayan Crisis: India, Nepal, China Must Act to Prevent Disaster - The Indian Awaaz
description: Himalayan Crisis: India, Nepal, China Must Act to Prevent Disaster  The Indian Awaaz
publisher.title: The Indian Awaaz
full_article:
Last Updated on October 23, 2026 4:24 pm by INDIAN AWAAZ

By Manan Kumar

The catastrophic flash floods in Nepal and Uttarkashi in the Himalayan region which claimed more than thounsand lives and left thousands missing, serve as a grim warning of what lies ahead. Geologists and climate scientists have warned that a strengthening El Niño cycle, superimposed on decades of accelerated global warming, could trigger an early and exceptionally intense summer across India, Nepal, and China in the summer of 2027.

Many experts like Professor Anil Kulkarni, leading glaciologist at the Divecha Centre for Climate Change Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and Saswat Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) have warned that rapid temperature increases and human-driven warming in the Himalayas will significantly raise the frequency of such catastrophic disasters.

This extreme thermal stress is expected to destabilize the high-altitude cryosphere (part of the Earth’s surface where water is in solid form, including ice, snow, glaciers, ice caps, ice sheets, and frozen ground) accelerating permafrost degradation, rapid glacial melting, and unprecedented slope instability. Consequently, the whole Himalayan region faces a heightened risk of cascading mountain hazards, including massive rock-ice avalanches, landslides, and catastrophic Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) during the ensuing monsoon season.

The Geography of Vulnerability

According to the Centre of Science and Environment (CSE) the rapid warming of the Western Himalayas is outpacing global averages resulting in the thawing of the deep permafrost that holds steep mountain walls together. Without this frozen structural glue, the risk of massive rockfalls, landslides, and debris flows spikes dramatically during summer.

The threat in the Himalayan region is not uniform. Certain geographic zones are highly vulnerable to these compounding climate drivers. In India, the states of Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, and Sikkim are on high alert. The Teesta River basin in Sikkim remains fragile following the devastating South Lhonak lake burst, while Uttarakhand’s steep valleys—home to major pilgrimage routes and massive infrastructure projects—face persistent landslide risks.

In Nepal, the risk is concentrated in the steep, narrow valleys of the Koshi, Gandaki, and Karnali river systems. Densely populated settlements situated downstream from rapidly expanding moraine-dammed lakes are highly exposed. For China, the Tibetan Plateau acts as the primary ground zero. Rising temperatures are causing rapid thermal erosion of Tibet’s high-altitude permafrost, which directly threatens critical regional transport links like the Qinghai-Tibet railway, alongside local engineering infrastructure.

The danger is amplified by the fact that these hazards are intrinsically transboundary. A glacial lake outburst or mountain collapse originating in the high-altitude valleys of Tibet in China can transform into a destructive flood wave within minutes, roaring through the deep gorges of Nepal and India before downstream populations can receive adequate warning.

Early Warning Systems are not enough

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has expanded its network to include dozens of Doppler weather radars, which significantly improve the tracking of localized cloudburst events. The regional digital portals like the Sachet and Flood Watch applications push automated, geo-fenced alerts to mobile users in vulnerable zones.

However, these systems cannot provide alerts before or at the exact time of flash-floods and are inadequate for the scale of the impending crises. High-altitude structural collapses and flash floods hurtle down steep vertical drops at immense speeds. During recent monsoon disasters, official alerts were generated only after monitoring stations were physically disrupted, giving downstream communities very little time to evacuate.

Furthermore, the lack of continuous, automated ground instrumentation at high elevations creates significant data scarcity. The most critical gap is institutional: the absence of a real-time, automated, cross-border data pipeline between China, Nepal, and India prevents early warnings from crossing political borders at the speed required to save lives.

A Tri-National Strategy for Mitigation

To prevent future calamities from culminating in widespread tragedy, the governments of India, Nepal, and China must move past political friction and establish an integrated, proactive disaster mitigation framework. Disaster management organizations like the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) emphasise that cross-border cooperation is essential for managing systemic climate risks in mountain ecosystems.

The three nations must formalize a binding, real-time hydrological data-sharing treaty. The current practice of sharing seasonal or manually transmitted data during emergencies is insufficient. Automated weather and water-level stations positioned near dangerous glacial lakes in Tibet and northern Nepal must be digitally linked directly to downstream emergency operation centers in India and lower Nepal, ensuring that an upstream surge triggers an instantaneous, automated broadcast to downstream villages.

Second, the three governments must pool resources to deploy advanced cryosphere tracking technologies. Utilizing high-resolution satellite Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) interferometry and frequent drone surveys will allow geologists to map micro-cracks and structural displacement in high-risk slopes before they completely fail. Identifying these structural weaknesses early provides the weeks of lead time necessary to conduct planned evacuations.

Third, engineering interventions must be scaled up to stabilize high-risk glacial lakes. This requires constructing controlled structural drainage channels, siphoning systems, and spillways to safely lower water volumes in unstable moraine-dammed lakes. Such projects require shared technical expertise and joint funding across borders, as stabilizing a lake in Tibet directly secures infrastructure and lives downriver in India and Nepal.

Finally, geologists and structural engineers working in the Himalayas agree that all three nations must implement strict, risk-informed land-use zoning. Mountain development must change fundamentally. Governments need to enforce strict expert moratoria on the construction of heavy infrastructure, including dense chains of run-of-the-river hydropower projects and massive highway expansions, above highly vulnerable elevations. In steep valleys, residential and tourism infrastructure must be moved to higher ground, well above the natural choke points where flash floods concentrate vertically.

Only through coordinated, transparent, and immediate tri-national action can the nations of the Himalaya protect their shared environment, infrastructure, and people.

Manan Kumar is a senior Journalist

KATHMANDU (Reuters) -- Rescuers recovered the bodies of two Japanese climbers missing since Oct. 15 on a Himalayan peak in northwest Nepal, an official said on Friday.

Kumar Chhetri of the Cosmo Adventure hiking company that provided local logistics to the Japanese climbers said the bodies were recovered from Gangapurna West peak, which is 7,140 meters high.

He did not give any details.

Arrangements are being made to send the bodies to a hospital in Kathmandu for postmortem, he said.

title: Nepal mixes tradition and technology for conservation - Nepali Times
description: Nepal mixes tradition and technology for conservation  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Four years ago, during a snow leopard expedition to Upper Dolpo a traditional medicine practitioner at the ancient Samling Monastery told me about the role this elusive Himalayan predator plays in local tradition.

Sherab Tenzin Lama is an ‘Amchi’ healer who has been practicing traditional medicine, a knowledge system passed down through generations. Over cups of a potent local drink alternated with hot water, the conversation progressed from snow leopards to the spaces that host them.

The rangelands of this remote trans-Himalayan region sustain the livestock on which communities depend, and they also support the prey base for snow leopards. People here raise yaks, sheep and mountain goats, harvest medicinal plants and earn money from trekking groups.

When World Wildlife Fund Nepal (WWF) began snow leopard conservation efforts in Upper Dolpo in 2018, livestock losses to wildlife were common. Improved corrals to protect sheep and yaks from predators, and a new approach to help victims access compensation for livestock losses have shown results.

Being an optimist, I imagined that successful management of human wildlife conflict was just a matter of time. And the outcome was indirectly proportional to the available resources. But that meant success would take a long time.

If wildlife kills decrease, would livestock density not increase? If it does, could the rangelands withstand additional grazing pressure? And, if so, what would happen to the people who depend on these mountains? What would be the effect on other wildlife like blue sheep and the snow leopards?

Having witnessed the changes over the decades, Amchi Sherab agreed that unmanaged rangeland use and over-extraction of natural resources would not be sustainable. Better road access, over-tourism and modern lifestyles and climatic breakdown added to the risks.

As a healer who depended on locally available herbs and medicinal plants, he had a practical outlook on the changes sweeping his land. Generations of native inhabitants have organically and conscientiously looked after this isolated region of Nepal using traditional knowledge, beliefs and values.

For instance, different parts of plants are used in Sowa Rigpa, the traditional science of healing. Plants are never uprooted, only a small proportion of flowers are collected leaving the rest for its propagation, and only parts of the roots are taken so that the plant does not die.

MOUNTAINS AND MINDS

“This is how we ensure that this plant is available for generations after us,” Amchi Sherab explained. That conversation four years ago left a strong impression on me. The knowledge for sustainable rangeland management existed, hidden deep in the mountains and in the minds of elders and faith leaders.

Back in Kathmandu, I began exploring how traditional knowledge about conservation could be supported to protect nature from new challenges. WWF had already been supported the Amchi of Dolpa in conserving medicinal plants.

One of the pioneers of this initiative was Yeshi Choden Lama, who along with Nepal's top conservationists was among 24 people killed in the helicopter crash at Ghunsa in the Kangchenjunga Conservation Area in September 2006.

With colleagues who shared this interest, WWF continued Yeshi Choden Lama’s work to support local youth, organising community consultations. The information was augmented through interviews with Amchi, monks, and elders.

TIn 2023, the Shey Phoksundo National Park (SPNP), Shey Phoksundo Rural Municipality (SPRM), faith leaders, and community youth came together to work towards integrated rangeland co-management.

In mid-2025, WWF was awarded the Darwin Initiative grant from the UK government to revive faith leadership for high mountain rangeland conservation in Nepal. Partners include Asia Network for Sustainable Agriculture and Bioresources (ANSAB) Nepal and Sowa Rigpa Association Nepal (SRAN).

This combines the community’s traditional knowledge with modern science, to create, build capacity and mobilise local institutions to collaborate on managing rangelands.

ANSAB supports sustainable harvesting of priority medicinal plants and helps elevate community earning through value chain optimisation and market linkage. SRAN helps the Amchi adapt the traditional practice to current circumstances so that this knowledge system is preserved and passed down.

Community-based rangeland conservation and management sub-committees consisting of youth, herders, women and faith leaders, have been formed. Harvesting and trade of medicinal plants have been initiated.

However, coordination among various groups in this remote landscape is challenging. The community’s socio-economic timelines are aligned to the seasons and packed tight, it allows for limited free time. Changing climate and increasingly unpredictable weather have disturbed the traditional timetable for these seasonal activities.

Snow leopards are at the top of the food chain, and protecting these elusive cats means sustaining local communities that hold nature in the highest regard and strengthening human-wildlife coexistence. Local livelihoods needs to be secure so the predators do not cause loss of livestock.

Zooming out of Dolpo, away from Nepal and toward High Mountain Asia, the larger challenge is to protect the ‘water tower’ that supports 2 billion people living downstream who depend on rivers that start here.

Friday, 23 October is Snow Leopard Day and 2026 also marks the International Year of the Rangelands and Pastoralists. It is an opportune time to remind ourselves of the interconnectedness of people and nature, and the part that human beings play in maintaining the natural order and systems.

The planet’s biodiversity is at a turning point. Yet, as indicated in WWF’s Living Planet Report 2026, there is hope. We can apply the knowledge of past generations with current technology to protect nature and enrich human life.

We can build a world where people thrive with nature. There is no alternative.

title: UN official: Nepal's flood recovery to take 2-3 years - NHKニュース
description: UN official: Nepal's flood recovery to take 2-3 years  NHKニュース
publisher.title: NHKニュース
full_article:
Two months after devastating floods and mudslides struck near the Nepal-China border, the top UN official in Nepal says recovery and reconstruction will take at least two to three years.

On the Nepal side, 1,457 deaths have been confirmed in the August 26 disaster and more than 5,200 people remain missing. On the Chinese side, media reports say the massive floods and mudslides killed 43 people, and at least 510 are still unaccounted for.

The UN resident coordinator, who is helping organize relief efforts in Nepal, spoke with NHK on Friday. Lila Pieters Yahia said while recovery work is ongoing in affected areas in central Nepal, such as Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, many residents are still displaced.

She said, "They are also stressed because a lot of people now are wondering what's going to happen to their livelihood and whether they will be able to have access to livelihood."

Yahia said many areas remain hard to access, so food and other essentials are being delivered using helicopters and drones.

She said a great many damaged structures have yet to be demolished and "enormous" amounts of rubble still need to be cleared.

The cleanup process "will take a long time," she said, calling on the international community for continued support.
